# Microsoft, Code-With Engineering Playbook: testing, code review, done and ready, non-functional requirements (selected sections)

**Source:** Microsoft (Industry Solutions Engineering), with contributors. *Code-With Engineering Playbook* (selected sections). https://microsoft.github.io/code-with-engineering-playbook/ ; repository at commit 016770e43d8a75be87b98c000c049f07c4a6e6f8 (2025-09-26). coverage: partial — operator-approved 2026-10-14 — selected sections of a 179,000-word playbook: automated testing (overview, test planning, unit, integration, end-to-end, consumer-driven contract, smoke and fault-injection testing), the whole code-reviews section, definition of done and of ready, and the non-functional requirements capture guide; performance, UI, shadow and synthetic-monitoring testing and the rest of the playbook are not taken

## Author's Thesis (condensed)

This light reference describes an operator-approved subset of the playbook, not the whole of it; every page in the subset was read in full for the deep reference, and pages the subset links to but does not hold are not described. The pages are practice guidance written largely in the first person plural, so their claims are the playbook's recommendations and assertions [AP]; they report no studies of their own, and where they lean on evidence it is a cited outside source [BT] or the authors' stated experience.

Tests are part of what makes code finished: "We consider code to be incomplete if it is not accompanied by tests" [V] (docs/automated-testing/README.md, "The Fundamentals"). Testing is a set of techniques, each suited to an outcome, arranged as a pyramid with most tests at the cheap, fast base [AP]. Peer review should happen on every pull request or check-in to a shared branch, with automation taking the mechanical checks so that human reviewers can concentrate on business logic, tests, readability and maintainability [AP] (docs/code-reviews/README.md, "Code Reviews"; docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/reviewer-guidance.md, "Reviewer Guidance"). Teams make completion and readiness explicit through a documented Definition of Done and Definition of Ready, and state non-functional requirements as "quantitative, measurable and testable" [V], early, when the cost of their impact on later design decisions is comparatively low (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "Documenting Non-Functional Requirements - Best Practices").

## Testing Fundamentals and Building for Testing

The overview gives four reasons to test: tests find flaws, document intent, save time over manual testing, and let a team refactor without regressions [AP]. Its fundamentals: unit tests (tests without external dependencies) can run before every PR merge; integration and end-to-end tests exercise the whole system and run regularly; "We write our tests early and block any further code merging if tests fail." [V]; and load or performance tests run where appropriate (docs/automated-testing/README.md, "Why Testing"; "The Fundamentals").

Applications should be built with testing in mind: parameterise values rather than hard-code them, log all parameters at startup, log to console and to an external system, log all activity with start and completion messages, pass a correlation ID between systems, log metadata such as tenant or order IDs, and record how long functions take [AP] (docs/automated-testing/README.md, "Build for Testing"). A map of outcomes to techniques points each validation goal (logical correctness, component interaction, composite scenarios, telemetry, security, compatibility, load, availability, recovery, resilience) to the techniques that serve it; several of the linked technique pages sit outside the subset [AP] (docs/automated-testing/README.md, "Map of Outcomes to Testing Techniques").

## Test Planning

Test cases are worked out while a user story is designed, to make sure all acceptance criteria are met, and the exercise "also helps clarify the acceptance criteria and informs how we should build the solution" [V] (docs/automated-testing/test-planning.md, "Building test cases for a user story"). The five steps are: understand the acceptance criteria and clarify ambiguities with the product owner; identify positive and negative scenarios and decide whether non-functional requirements are in scope; define test cases (title, preconditions, steps, expected result), optionally in Given-When-Then form; automate where possible, focusing on hot paths and critical areas; and review the cases with peers or stakeholders [AP]. Five example cases include a login protected against SQL injection and a system that maintains 99.9% uptime over a month [AE].

Test cases group into plans (full regression, smoke, functional and area regression, plus integration, user acceptance, load, security, compatibility, recovery and localization), which the page says bring clear scope, systematic execution and a risk-based focus on the most critical areas [AP]. A full regression plan includes all previously reported bugs that have been fixed [AP] (docs/automated-testing/test-planning.md, "Grouping Test Cases into Test Plans"; "Common Test Plans"; "Other Test Plan Examples").

## Unit Testing

A unit test should be provably reliable, fast and isolated: it "should be 100% reliable so failures indicate a bug in the code" [V], a whole suite should take no longer than a couple of seconds, and external dependencies are removed (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Unit Testing"). The reasons given are lower cost (a production bug is estimated, in a cited outside study, to cost about six times as much as one caught in implementation [BT]), developer confidence, faster development through early feedback in the inner loop, and tests as documentation that runs with every build [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/why-unit-tests.md, "Why Unit Tests").

The techniques are abstraction (break a hard dependency behind a concept), dependency injection (used intentionally, since it "can easily go overboard" [V]) and test-driven development, which "will lead you to a testable design from the start" [V] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Abstraction"; "Dependency Injection"; "Test-Driven Development"). Best practices are Arrange/Act/Assert, small tests that test one thing, and a consistent descriptive naming convention; things to avoid are sleeps, reading from disk and calling third-party APIs, each of which breaks speed, isolation or reliability [AP]. Abstracted dependencies stay uncovered, so integration or functional tests are still needed, and "Unit testing is extremely important, but it is also not the silver bullet" [V] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Abstraction"; "Things to Avoid"; "Conclusion"). In some situations, integration tests fast enough for the inner loop can take over coverage, verifying behaviour as well as wiring [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Transferring Responsibility to Integration Tests").

Two worked examples show the practice. The TDD page builds a password validator one test at a time, writing "the bare minimum of code necessary" [V] to pass each test before refactoring [AE] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/tdd-example.md, "Test-Driven Development Example"). The authoring page abstracts a file-reading configuration class behind an interface, injects it, and finds that its first tests reached 100% coverage while a bug still showed that not all inputs were covered; new tests stating the intended behaviour leave 4 failing and 1 passing until the fix [AE] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/authoring-example.md, "Fixing the Bug").

## Test Doubles

Stubs return predetermined behaviour and "should never fail a unit or integration test where a mock can" [V]; mocks carry expectations about calls, so "mocks do behavioral verification, whereas other test doubles do state verification" [V]; fakes are working shortcuts such as an in-memory database (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Stubs"; "Mocks"; "Fakes"). The page's objection to behavioural verification is that it ties a test to the implementation, so tests must change whenever the implementation does, and the confidence that a passing test signals a safe change is lost [AP]. Its rule for assertions: "make assertions on your logic, not mock return values" [V], since a test that only checks what the mock returned would pass even if the method returned a literal [AE] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Assertions"). It recommends starting without a mocking framework and writing fakes where possible [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Conclusion").

## Integration, End-to-End and Contract Tests

Integration tests check that separately developed components work together, exposing issues such as broken database schemas or faulty third-party integrations [AP]; they are fewer, slower and costlier than unit tests, and can run early and often with mock data [AP] (docs/automated-testing/integration-testing/README.md, "Why Integration Testing"; "Integration Testing Design Blocks"). The page warns against too many or over-mocked integration tests, against business logic in integration tests, and against writing them in production: use "a scaled-down copy environment" [V] (docs/automated-testing/integration-testing/README.md, "Things to Avoid"). This sits in some tension with the unit-testing page's option of shifting business-logic coverage to integration tests.

End-to-end tests run a whole application flow across sub-systems in a production-like environment, through formal planning, execution and closure, with metrics for preparation, progress, defects and environment availability [AP] (docs/automated-testing/e2e-testing/README.md, "Applying the E2E Testing"; "Test Metrics"). Higher-pyramid tests are fewer, slower and costlier, and end-to-end tests are often run by hand [AP]. A comparison table sets unit, integration, system and end-to-end tests against scope, environment, data and timing; for end-to-end it lists a copy of real production data [AP] (docs/automated-testing/e2e-testing/testing-comparison.md, "Unit vs Integration vs System vs E2E Testing"). Consumer-driven contract tests let consumers define the responses they expect against a provider mock, generate a versioned contract, and verify it against the real provider in a separate pipeline, so a failure points to either wrong consumer expectations or a broken provider [AP]. "Contracts are not a replacement for a discussion between the consumer and provider team." [V] (docs/automated-testing/cdc-testing/README.md, "Contract").

## Smoke and Fault-Injection Tests

Smoke tests are quick gates on the most critical path that tell a pipeline whether to go on; if they fail, the rest of the integration or deployment chain can be abandoned [AP] (docs/automated-testing/smoke-testing/README.md, "Problem Addressed"). They apply on the desktop, in build pipelines, before and after deployments and in PR validation, and the page calls them "a low-effort, high-impact step to ship more reliable software" [V] (docs/automated-testing/smoke-testing/README.md, "Conclusion").

Fault injection deliberately introduces faults at the software, protocol and infrastructure levels to harden a system against failure [AP]. It runs in the development cycle (fuzzing in CI, regression and acceptance tests written from fixed issues or resolved incidents) and in the release cycle against live systems [AP]. Because a failed experiment in production will likely affect customers, "Thinking about the Blast Radius of the effect, should the test fail, is a crucial step to conduct beforehand." [V]; the advice is to start outside production, gate CD stages with it, use blue/green and canary deployments, agree a budget as a service level objective, and grow risk in layers locked in by regression tests [AP] (docs/automated-testing/fault-injection-testing/README.md, "Best Practices and Advice").

## Code Review Goals and Process

Review has three goals: remove defects before they reach shared branches, learn and grow, and build shared understanding of the code [AP] (docs/code-reviews/README.md, "Goals"). Teams should review in a timely way, set a review service-level agreement, measure time to merge, and automate linting, analysis, builds and tests so reviewers need not chase nits [AP]. On size: "More code there is to review, the higher chances there are letting a bug sneak through." [V] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/README.md, "Code Reviews Shouldn't Include too Many Lines of Code").

Authors describe the PR, add relevant reviewers (including someone less familiar, to spread knowledge), resolve each comment or mark it "won't fix" with reasons, and do not defer in-scope changes [AP] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/author-guidance.md, "Add Relevant Reviewers"; "Be Open to Receive Feedback"). Reviewers "Read every line changed." [V], keep to scope ("Don't block the current PR due to issues that are out of scope." [V]), and run a design pass and then a code-quality pass covering complexity, naming, error handling, functionality (including security flaws and PII handling), style and tests; tests come in the same PR as the code (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/reviewer-guidance.md, "Understand the Code You are Reviewing"; "Take Your Time and Keep Focus on Scope"; "Code Quality Pass"). For pairs, "Someone outside the pair should perform the code review." [V] (docs/code-reviews/faq.md, "We Pair or Mob. How Should This Reflect in our Code Reviews?").

## Pull Requests, Evidence and Inclusion

"Changes to any main codebase - main branch in Git repository, for example - must be done using pull requests (PR)." [V] PR requirements "can and should be enforced by policies" [V] (docs/code-reviews/pull-requests.md, "Pull Requests"). Before opening a PR the code should compile and run without errors or warnings, with all new and existing tests passing; PRs should be small, focused on one reason to change, and never break the build [AP] (docs/code-reviews/pull-requests.md, "General Process"; "Size Guidance"; "Best Practices"). The PR template asks for the work item, the change and its impact, bug reproduction steps, a checklist (tests added, tests passed, no new lint errors or warnings), whether the change is breaking and its migration path, testing instructions and relevant logs [AP] (docs/code-reviews/pull-request-template.md, "Pull Request Template").

Branch policies "may be sufficient evidence that a project team is conducting code reviews" [V]; the evidence checklist adds linked bug-to-PR records noting how review might have caught each bug, and regularly updated review checklists [AP] (docs/code-reviews/evidence-and-measures/README.md, "Evidence"). The inclusion page treats review conduct as part of review quality, naming inequitable assignment, long subjective arguments and bias about the developer rather than the code (for instance, assuming one developer's code is always good) as non-inclusive behaviour [AP] (docs/code-reviews/inclusion-in-code-review.md, "Types and Examples of Non-Inclusive Code Review Behavior").

## Definition of Done and Definition of Ready

"The development team should decide together what their Definition of Done is and document this in the project." [V] Its example story-level checks include acceptance criteria met, unit tests written and passing, code review complete, sufficient diagnostics and telemetry logged, documentation updated and product-owner sign-off; sprint and release levels add functional, integration, performance and end-to-end tests passing and a release marked ready by the product owner [AP] (docs/agile-development/team-agreements/definition-of-done.md, "Feature/User Story"; "Sprint Goal"; "Release/Milestone").

A story is Ready when it has enough detail to estimate within the sprint, and "If a user story is not Ready in the beginning of the Sprint it increases the chance that the story will not be done at the end of this sprint." [V] Example items: input values, clear and measurable acceptance criteria, business need, a size that fits a short time, and known blockers [AP] (docs/agile-development/team-agreements/definition-of-ready.md, "Definition of Ready"; "Examples of Ready Checklist Items").

## Non-Functional Requirements

Non-functional requirements, "also known as quality attributes" [V], say how a system performs its functions under given conditions; defining them early lets them be weighed while their impact on later design is cheap [AP] (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "Goals"). Each should be specific, tied to business objectives, scoped to a component or process, and traded off openly [AP]. The capture template records name, description, priority, metric, verification method (automated test, benchmark, simulation, prototyping), constraints, owner and dependencies [AP]. A taxonomy covers operational, performance, security and compliance, maintainability and user-experience attributes, each with example metrics and thresholds that are illustrative, not measured [AP] (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "Template"; "Examples").

All figures are the playbook's own statements; apart from the borrowed cost estimate, they are recommendations or illustrative examples, not measurements.

| Metric | Value | Class |
|---|---|---|
| Unit test reliability | "should be 100% reliable so failures indicate a bug in the code" | [V] |
| Unit suite speed | "should run in milliseconds, a whole unit testing suite shouldn't take longer than a couple seconds" | [V] |
| Production bug cost vs implementation | about 6 times as much (cited outside study) | [BT] |
| Reviewer complexity heuristic | "If a method has greater than 3 arguments, it is potentially overly complex." | [V] |
| Uptime and allowed downtime per year | 99% ≈ 3.65 days; 99.9% ≈ 8.76 hours; 99.99% ≈ 52.56 minutes; 99.999% ≈ 5.26 minutes | [AP] |
| Example maintainability thresholds | cyclomatic complexity under 10 or under 50 lines per function; 80% or higher coverage commonly targeted; code churn under 20% | [AP] example |
| Example performance targets | 500 ms response; 100 concurrent users or 500 transactions per second; error rate under 1% | [AP] example |
| Configuration worked example | 4 failing, 1 passing after the intended behaviour is specified | [AE] |

## Key Connections

The pages draw on outside work, all of it borrowed-through and not held in this corpus [BT]:

- An outside author's definitions of test doubles and mocks, adopted by the mocking page.
- Outside blog posts as the source of the testing-pyramid figure and of the claim that many teams write too many end-to-end tests.
- An outside article for the consumer-driven contract approach, and an outside tool described as the de-facto standard for contract testing.
- An outside study for the six-times production-bug cost estimate.
- Outside principles of chaos experimentation, an outside security lifecycle's fuzzing requirement, and an outside outage as a caution about blast radius.
- Outside guides on code review, code inspection and PR size, and a commit-message convention, listed as resources.

## Signature Contrarian Positions

1. Heavy reliance on mocking frameworks and behavioural verification produces tests tied to the implementation; start without a framework and write fakes where possible.
2. Teams write too many end-to-end tests; contract tests can cover most component interactions, keeping some end-to-end tests for the deployed whole.
3. Unit testing is not sufficient on its own: abstracted dependencies stay uncovered.
4. Deferring work is named as unacceptable: tests come with the code, not in a later PR, and in-scope review comments are fixed now, not later [AP] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/reviewer-guidance.md, "Tests"; docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/author-guidance.md, "Be Open to Receive Feedback").
5. Large, unfocused PRs and huge commits lead to weak and unfair review.
6. Out-of-scope issues should not block the current PR; they become separate work items.
7. The cost of code review is "actually negative!" [V], because defects removed in review cost far less than defects found in production (docs/code-reviews/evidence-and-measures/README.md, "Measures").
